source.title: Beyond receptive fields: sequence-pooled normalization can supply most of a sequence labeler's context

page_placements.theme: Ablation compared with retraining and observational estimates: ablation can overstate as well as understate

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; not garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses adaptation and compensation after removal, citing McGrath et al. (2023), but its own experiments do not test downstream self-repair in language models. Its ablation experiments concern convolutional sequence-labeling blocks and a separate normalization-path confound.
record.gate_note: The paper reports block-ablation and retraining results for convolutional sequence labelers. These measure an attribution discrepancy caused by removing sequence-pooled normalization with the blocks, not later components changing outputs to restore a prediction. The results are recorded under fits_no_version; cited self-repair results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses dilated convolutional sequence labelers, not language models. It does not ablate attention layers or heads, MLPs or LayerNorm in a transformer LM, and does not measure later components restoring the output. It cites McGrath et al. (2023) only to name an ordinary ablation-versus-retraining gap. That gap is the 1.1–1.3× ratio under per-position normalization, which mixes retraining adaptation with compensation and is not separated or measured as self-repair. Its main finding is that block ablation severs a sequence-pooled normalization path. That is a different mechanism from self-repair, in a different kind of system, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that sequence-pooled normalization gives conv sequence labelers context beyond their receptive field. They also conclude that ablating reach-enlarging blocks overstates those blocks' contribution by roughly an order of magnitude, because the ablation severs that path. They attribute the residual 1.1–1.3× gap under per-position normalization to adaptation and compensation.
record.recipe_differences: The study removes groups of convolutional blocks from trained sequence-labeling networks and compares with retraining; it does not ablate language-model attention layers or heads or measure self-repair. Not a replication of the original method.
record.method_sensitivity: The attribution discrepancy changes with normalization pooling axes (sequence-pooled versus per-position) and task difficulty; the paper also varies block-removal cut and data setting.

fits_no_version.finding: In a dilated conv stack, ablating long-range blocks costs 8.3× (simulation) to 16.1× (real haplotypes) more accuracy than retraining without them when normalization pools along the sequence. With per-position statistics the ratio is about 1.0–1.5×.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ablation overstates a component's contribution when removing it also removes a shared sequence-spanning normalization path.

fits_no_version.finding: At a shallower cut (dilation ≥ 8), ablation retention falls from 0.79 to 0.28 as difficulty rises. Retraining retention moves only from 0.97 to 0.90.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ablation-based and retraining-based retention estimates show different trends across task difficulty in sequence-pooled conv labelers.

record.problems: The study uses three seeds. The real-data arm uses one chromosome and one population pair, with replicates sharing chromosome-specific properties. It removes groups of convolutional blocks rather than single attention components and does not measure component-output changes or restoration of the original prediction by later components.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted duplicate headline and Table 2 versions of the ablation/retraining comparisons, since their per-level values are captured from Table F.11. Omitted figure-only plotted values where the text and tables report the same result.

untested.parts: Attention-layer ablation and downstream attention-layer compensation in language models.
Late-MLP downregulation of the maximum-likelihood token and its change under earlier ablations.
Single-head ablation with compensation on general text across LM families and sizes.
Partial, prompt-variable and overcorrecting self-repair in LMs.
Backup heads, copy-suppression heads, final LayerNorm rescaling, anti-erasure neurons.
Self-repair under mean or resample ablation versus zero ablation.
Whether LM self-repair makes ablation importance scores misstate component function. The paper shows ablation overstating CNN block contributions via a normalization path, not via self-repair.

record.verdict_notes: Row values match Table F.11 and the Section 6 text, so no row fixes are needed. McGrath et al. is cited as related work only; the paper makes no measurement of LM self-repair.

versions.untested_parts: Layer-level attention ablation and downstream attention-layer compensation in language models.
Late-MLP effects on maximum-likelihood tokens and how they change under earlier ablations.
Single attention-head ablation and compensation on full output distributions across language models.
Prompt-level variation and overcorrection in language-model self-repair.
Backup heads, copy-suppression heads, final LayerNorm rescaling, and anti-erasure neurons.
Self-repair under mean or resample ablations.
Whether self-repair causes ablation-based importance scores to misstate language-model component function.
